title: Maternal Response to Physical Exercise
summary:
This chapter explains how the pregnant body responds to a single exercise session (acute response) and to regular training over time (chronic adaptation). During exercise the body must keep blood flowing to active muscles, protect uteroplacental blood flow, and regulate temperature and metabolism.

Acute responses include faster heart rate rise, greater cardiac output, deeper breathing, more fat use, better insulin sensitivity and extra heat production. Uteroplacental flow stays stable at moderate intensity, and fetal heart rate may rise 10-20 bpm, returning to baseline within 5 minutes. Chronic training improves cardiovascular efficiency, glucose control, strength, balance and well-being, with benefits for the fetus such as lower risk of macrosomia and cesarean section. The authors conclude that the pregnant body is efficient and adaptable, and that training should be adapted to stage, level and need.
points: Each session must maintain muscle perfusion, protect uteroplacental blood flow and regulate body temperature and metabolism.
Cardiac output may increase by an additional 30%-40% during exercise, and heart rate rises faster and higher than in nonpregnant women under the same load.
Maximum heart rate is usually reduced in pregnancy, so it should not be the sole intensity indicator; the Borg scale (RPE 12-14) and the talk test are recommended.
Prioritize moderate intensities of 50%-70% of VO2max.
Basal temperature rises slightly (0.3 C-0.5 C), and exercise adds metabolic heat.
Above 85% of maximum heart rate, uteroplacental flow may be temporarily reduced, so vigorous intensities are not recommended without medical supervision.
Fetal heart rate may increase 10-20 bpm during maternal exertion and returns to baseline within 5 minutes; no signs of fetal distress were found in healthy women training in a controlled manner.
Weight-bearing activity such as treadmill walking causes higher VO2 in pregnant women than cycle ergometry.
Regular exercise improves glycemic and lipid control, strength, balance and well-being, and in the fetus reduces the risk of macrosomia and cesarean section.
takeaways: Use RPE 12-14 and the talk test rather than heart rate alone to set intensity.
Avoid prolonged fasting before training and have a light intake of complex carbohydrates before and after exercise.
Train in cool, well-ventilated settings with breathable clothing and good hydration.
Strengthen core, gluteal and stabilizing muscles, and add proprioception and balance training; avoid jumping and sudden impacts.
Add conscious breathing work such as yoga or mindfulness, and avoid the Valsalva maneuver.
Individualize sessions by trimester, check vital signs before and after, include core, pelvic floor and breathing work, and coordinate with an obstetrician or physical therapist.
cautions: Avoid hot or humid environments because of the thermoregulation load.
Monitor time spent lying on the back, since prolonged supine exercise reduces venous return and uterine flow.
Avoid Valsalva and other exercises that cause apnea.
Do not use vigorous intensities above 85% of maximum heart rate without medical supervision.
